tools.name: betterstack-noesis__catalog_relations
tools.description:
List the catalog's relations with their primary and added attributes and how many records each holds.

## How the catalog works

The catalog adds business context to incidents through lookup tables.

- A **relation** is a table. Its **primary attributes** are the key columns, its **added attributes** are the columns it adds, and each **record** is a row.
- A primary attribute is named after a metadata key incidents already carry, set by a monitor, an integration, the reporter or another relation. When an incident's value for that key equals a record's primary value exactly, the record's added values are copied onto the incident as metadata, where escalation policies can act on them.
- With several primary attributes, the relation's matching decides: `any` matches a record when one of its primary values matches, `all` only when every primary attribute does, an empty primary cell matching anything there. A record with every primary cell empty is the relation's fallback, used only when no other record matches.
- A value is text, or a Better Stack object: `Team`, `User` (a team member), `Policy` (an escalation policy), `Schedule` (an on-call calendar), `Endpoint` (a monitor) and more. Reference an object by `name` (a team member by `email`) or by the `item_id` that `catalog_relation` shows, a monitor by `item_id` only; the team IDs other tools take are a different number.
- An added attribute named like another relation's primary attribute chains the lookup: the value it adds is looked up in that relation next.
- Three added attributes draw the Dependencies map on Integrations → Catalog:
  - `Dependencies`: the records this one needs, named by their primary value. An incident on any of them marks this record as affected too.
  - `Connections`: the records this one talks to, drawn without passing incidents on.
  - `Type`: Database, Storage, Frontend, Backend, Mobile app or Desktop app, which sets the record's icon.

Read one relation's records with `catalog_relation`.

per_page.description: Number of relations per page (default: 50, max: 250)

tools.description:
Execute a ClickHouse SQL query to retrieve logs, traces/spans, errors, and metrics from telemetry data.

Write the query as a template and the server builds the collections for you, as Better Stack's dashboards and AI SRE do:
- `FROM {{source}}` reads the source's recent and historical rows of `source_type` together (for metrics, its metrics collection), scoped to the source
- `{{start_time}}` and `{{end_time}}` are the `start_time` and `end_time` arguments, e.g. `WHERE dt >= {{start_time}} AND dt < {{end_time}}`
- `{{time}}` buckets `dt` to an interval that suits the range (`toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL '<n> second')`); `{{interval_seconds}}` is that interval
A template needs `source_type`, `start_time` and `end_time`, and no `table`. A query without `{{...}}` runs exactly as written, needs `table` and must name its `remote(...)` and `s3Cluster(...)` collections itself.

- **IMPORTANT**: Use `query_help` to get instructions on how to create the correct query for logs and spans
- **IMPORTANT**: Use `errors_query_help` to get instructions on how to create the correct query for errors
- **IMPORTANT**: Use `metrics_query_help` to get instructions on how to create the correct query for metrics
- Before a query over more than a few hours of logs, spans or other events, call `query_windows` with the same arguments: it says whether the range fits one call and, if not, the time windows that do. A template of either shape below needs no such call: `query` splits its range itself

tools.name: betterstack-noesis__query_windows
tools.description:
Size an S3 query before running it: how many rows its time range holds and, when that is more than one `query` call reads (50,000,000 rows, 50 seconds), the time windows that fit one call each.

Pass the same arguments you would pass to `query` (`query`, `source_id`, and `table` for SQL without template variables or `source_type`, `start_time` and `end_time` for a template). Nothing is read from S3; the answer comes from the source's row counts in well under a second.

All timestamps are UTC; when `server_timezone` is not UTC, write each bound as toDateTime('<value>', 'UTC') rather than as a bare literal, which would be parsed in the server's timezone.

Every answer with a `decision` carries `notes`, what it says to do, written for this query: how to pass and merge its windows, what to replace before splitting a template that uses `{{time}}`, why the range could not be sized.

Returns `decision`:
- `run` — the range fits one call; run the query as written
- `windows` — Run the query once per window, newest first, with `dt >= '<from>' AND dt < '<to>'` in place of its time filter, and merge the results yourself: rows concatenate; `count()` and `sum()` add up; `min()` and `max()` combine; an average needs `sum()` and `count()` per window; `quantile(...)`, `uniq(...)`, `count(DISTINCT ...)` and `topK(...)` do not merge across windows, so keep those to one window or add filters. For a template whose time filter is `{{start_time}}`/`{{end_time}}`, pass each window as `start_time` = `from` and `end_time` = `to` instead. When `query` splits such a template itself (its description names the two shapes), `notes` says to call `query` once instead, and the windows are only a fallback. At most 200 windows are returned; `more_windows` counts the older ones the range still holds. More windows than you will run means the range needs rethinking: narrow the time filter, add filters on `raw` before extracting JSON, or set `sampling=` to `suggested_sampling` to estimate rather than measure. A window marked `oversized` holds more than the budget in a single second: add filters or `sampling=` for it
- `unsized` — the query's shape cannot be sized; `explanation` says what to change

With `run` or `windows`:
- `hot_tail` (never for a `{{source}}` template or a query that reads the hot collection itself with `remote()`) — the newest rows of the range are still in the hot collection, which `s3Cluster` holds only once they leave it: `from` is the oldest row still there (Live tail's first row on disk), `estimated_rows` how many of the range's rows that is, `collection` the hot collection to read them from when the row type names one; the top-level `estimated_rows` and the windows then count S3 rows only. Run the same query against `remote(<collection>)` with the time filter unchanged and no `_row_type` filter, and merge it in as one more window. The windows deliberately read past `from`, so a row uploaded to S3 since then is in both legs: add `AND dt < <from>` to them when the merged `count()` or `sum()` has to be exact. Without `from` the boundary could not be probed and the range merely reaches into the last hours
- `hot_rows` (a `{{source}}` template, or a query that reads the hot collection itself, whose range is over the budget with its hot rows counted) — how many rows of the range are still in the hot collection: the query reads them too, but `estimated_rows` and the budget leave them out, since a hot read is usually fast. Without `hot_rows`, `estimated_rows` counts them. If the query still times out on them, the timeout lists windows that split them
- `suggested_sampling` — with more windows than you will run, the `sampling=` rate at which the whole range fits one call

tools.name: betterstack-noesis__render_chart
tools.description:
Execute a ClickHouse SQL query and visualize the result as a chart.

Use `chart_type` to choose the visualization:
- `line` (default) — trends over time. Alias columns as `time`, `value`, and optional `series`.
- `bar` — magnitude over time or across buckets. Uses the same columns as `line`; set `stacked: true` to stack the series.
- `pie` — share of a total across categories. Alias a categorical column `AS series` (the slice label) and a numeric column `AS value` (the slice size), e.g. `SELECT service AS series, count() AS value FROM ... GROUP BY service`.

Write the query as a template and the server builds the collections for you, as Better Stack's dashboards and AI SRE do:
- `FROM {{source}}` reads the source's recent and historical rows of `source_type` together (for metrics, its metrics collection), scoped to the source
- `{{start_time}}` and `{{end_time}}` are the `start_time` and `end_time` arguments, e.g. `WHERE dt >= {{start_time}} AND dt < {{end_time}}`
- `{{time}}` buckets `dt` to an interval that suits the range (`toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL '<n> second')`); `{{interval_seconds}}` is that interval
A template needs `source_type`, `start_time` and `end_time`, and no `table`. A query without `{{...}}` runs exactly as written, needs `table` and must name its `remote(...)` and `s3Cluster(...)` collections itself.

Alias result columns as (line/bar):
- `... AS time` — the time bucket (e.g., `{{time}} AS time` in a template, or `toStartOfHour(dt) AS time`)
- `... AS value` — the numeric metric (e.g., `count() AS value`)
- `... AS series` — optional: a grouping column for multiple series (e.g., `service AS series`)

**IMPORTANT (line/bar): Always choose a time granularity that produces 50–500 data points** (`{{time}}` picks 30 seconds to 2 hours from the range, which is in that band up to a day but gives more points on longer ranges: bucket by hand there) — too few points make the chart useless, too many make it unreadable. Use these rules based on the query's time range:
- Up to 1 hour → `toStartOfMinute(dt) AS time` → ~60 points
- 1–24 hours → `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 5 MINUTE) AS time` → up to 288 points
- 1–7 days → `toStartOfHour(dt) AS time` → up to 168 points
- 7–30 days → `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 4 HOUR) AS time` → up to 180 points
- 30–90 days → `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 12 HOUR) AS time` → up to 180 points
- 90+ days → `toStartOfDay(dt) AS time`

Additional query instructions (data access patterns) are in:
- `query_help` — logs and spans
- `errors_query_help` — errors
- `metrics_query_help` — metrics

Before a query over more than a few hours of logs, spans or other events, call `query_windows` with the same arguments: it says whether the range fits one call and, if not, the time windows that do.

tools.description:
Add a new chart to a dashboard. Use the `section` parameter to organize charts into named sections — sections are auto-created if they don't exist, and charts are auto-positioned within them.

**REQUIRED**: the `query`'s FROM must reference a source, either `{{source}}` or a source-type variable defined via `set_dashboard_variable` (e.g. `{{redis_source}}`). A query with no source is rejected with guidance to define it first.

Dashboard chart queries run against the metrics collection: use `sum(logs_count)` (or the matching `sum(<row_type>_count)` for the source), `avgMerge(value_avg)`, `label('tag')`. Do NOT use `JSONExtract(raw, …)` — that is for live-tail charts and `query` only; dashboards have no `raw` column. Call `metrics_query_help` with the source ID **and `context: 'chart_query'`** for available metrics/labels and chart-query-style examples.

**Workflow:**
1. Call `chart_building_help` for chart types, units, and settings.
2. Call `metrics_query_help` with `context: 'chart_query'` to see the source's metrics schema and chart-query examples.
3. Verify the query with `render_chart` (runs it and surfaces errors automatically) or with `query`.

Use `{{source}}`, `{{start_time}}`, `{{end_time}}`, `{{time}}` variables for integration with dashboard filters. Queries can also reference custom dashboard variables — `{{var}}` (required) or `[[ AND col = {{var}} ]]` (optional clause, dropped while the variable is empty); define them with `set_dashboard_variable`.

Its FROM must reference a source: {{source}}, or a source-type variable defined via set_dashboard_variable (e.g. {{redis_source}}); hardcoded collection names are rejected. Use {{start_time}}/{{end_time}} in the time filter and {{time}} for bucketing. Dashboard charts query the metrics collection (use sum(logs_count) / sum(spans_count) / sum(exceptions_count) / sum(replays_count) / sum(web_events_count) / sum(metrics_count) for type-specific counts, avgMerge(value_avg), label('tag')); JSONExtract(raw, …) only works in live-tail charts.

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__catalog_relations
tools.description:
List the catalog's relations with their primary and added attributes and how many records each holds.

## How the catalog works

The catalog adds business context to incidents through lookup tables.

- A **relation** is a table. Its **primary attributes** are the key columns, its **added attributes** are the columns it adds, and each **record** is a row.
- A primary attribute is named after a metadata key incidents already carry, set by a monitor, an integration, the reporter or another relation. When an incident's value for that key equals a record's primary value exactly, the record's added values are copied onto the incident as metadata, where escalation policies can act on them.
- With several primary attributes, the relation's matching decides: `any` matches a record when one of its primary values matches, `all` only when every primary attribute does, an empty primary cell matching anything there. A record with every primary cell empty is the relation's fallback, used only when no other record matches.
- A value is text, or a Better Stack object: `Team`, `User` (a team member), `Policy` (an escalation policy), `Schedule` (an on-call calendar), `Endpoint` (a monitor) and more. Reference an object by `name` (a team member by `email`) or by the `item_id` that `catalog_relation` shows, a monitor by `item_id` only; the team IDs other tools take are a different number.
- An added attribute named like another relation's primary attribute chains the lookup: the value it adds is looked up in that relation next.
- Three added attributes draw the Dependencies map on Integrations → Catalog:
  - `Dependencies`: the records this one needs, named by their primary value. An incident on any of them marks this record as affected too.
  - `Connections`: the records this one talks to, drawn without passing incidents on.
  - `Type`: Database, Storage, Frontend, Backend, Mobile app or Desktop app, which sets the record's icon.

Read one relation's records with `catalog_relation`.

per_page.description: Number of relations per page (default: 50, max: 250)

tools.description:
Create a catalog relation with its primary and added attributes in one call. Add records with
`upsert_catalog_records` afterwards. See `catalog_relations` for how the catalog works.

Propose the relation to the user first (its name, matching, attributes and a few example records)
and create it once they agree. For a relation describing services, add `Dependencies`,
`Connections` and `Type` as added attributes, so the Dependencies map can draw its records.

- Name primary attributes after metadata keys incidents really carry. Check recent incidents' metadata with `incidents` and `incident` first: a key no incident carries never matches.

- Never invent records. Every row comes from a source the user pointed you to (code, Terraform, Kubernetes, a Backstage catalog, the service map) or from the user.
- Prefer `upsert_catalog_records` to removing records and adding them again: it keeps every record it doesn't name, while removing them all empties the relation.

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__delete_catalog_records
tools.description:
Remove catalog records by their primary values, or every record of a relation with `all: true`. A
record is removed when its primary values equal a given row's, as `upsert_catalog_records` matches
them; a row matching several records removes none of them. See `catalog_relations` for how the catalog works.

- Name primary attributes after metadata keys incidents really carry. Check recent incidents' metadata with `incidents` and `incident` first: a key no incident carries never matches.
- Reference teams, team members, escalation policies and other Better Stack objects as objects, like `{"type": "Team", "name": "Platform"}`, never as their names in text.
- Never invent records. Every row comes from a source the user pointed you to (code, Terraform, Kubernetes, a Backstage catalog, the service map) or from the user.

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__query
tools.description:
Execute a ClickHouse SQL query to retrieve logs, traces/spans, errors, and metrics from telemetry data.

Write the query as a template and the server builds the collections for you, as Better Stack's dashboards and AI SRE do:
- `FROM {{source}}` reads the source's recent and historical rows of `source_type` together (for metrics, its metrics collection), scoped to the source
- `{{start_time}}` and `{{end_time}}` are the `start_time` and `end_time` arguments, e.g. `WHERE dt >= {{start_time}} AND dt < {{end_time}}`
- `{{time}}` buckets `dt` to an interval that suits the range (`toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL '<n> second')`); `{{interval_seconds}}` is that interval
A template needs `source_type`, `start_time` and `end_time`, and no `table`. A query without `{{...}}` runs exactly as written, needs `table` and must name its `remote(...)` and `s3Cluster(...)` collections itself.

- **IMPORTANT**: Use `query_help` to get instructions on how to create the correct query for logs and spans
- **IMPORTANT**: Use `errors_query_help` to get instructions on how to create the correct query for errors
- **IMPORTANT**: Use `metrics_query_help` to get instructions on how to create the correct query for metrics
- Before a query over more than a few hours of logs, spans or other events, call `query_windows` with the same arguments: it says whether the range fits one call and, if not, the time windows that do. A template of either shape below needs no such call: `query` splits its range itself
- A template listing the newest rows (`ORDER BY dt DESC LIMIT n`, filtered by `dt >= {{start_time}} AND dt < {{end_time}}`, with no aggregate, `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT` or subquery) whose range is too wide for one call is read one time window at a time, newest first, until it has its n rows; the result says how far it read and where to continue
- A template that only adds up or combines (`count()`, `countIf()`, `sum()`, `sumIf()`, `min()`, `max()`, beside the `GROUP BY` columns it selects; `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` on those), filtered by `dt >= {{start_time}} AND dt < {{end_time}}`, with no `HAVING`, `DISTINCT` or subquery, whose range is too wide for one call but holds at most 300,000,000 rows is run in time windows, several at once, and the windows' rows merged; the result says how far it read

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__query_windows
tools.description:
Size an S3 query before running it: how many rows its time range holds and, when that is more than one `query` call reads (50,000,000 rows, 50 seconds), the time windows that fit one call each.

Pass the same arguments you would pass to `query` (`query`, `source_id`, and `table` for SQL without template variables or `source_type`, `start_time` and `end_time` for a template). Nothing is read from S3; the answer comes from the source's row counts in well under a second.

All timestamps are UTC; when `server_timezone` is not UTC, write each bound as toDateTime('<value>', 'UTC') rather than as a bare literal, which would be parsed in the server's timezone.

Every answer with a `decision` carries `notes`, what it says to do, written for this query: how to pass and merge its windows, what to replace before splitting a template that uses `{{time}}`, why the range could not be sized.

Returns `decision`:
- `run` — the range fits one call; run the query as written
- `windows` — Run the query once per window, newest first, with `dt >= '<from>' AND dt < '<to>'` in place of its time filter, and merge the results yourself: rows concatenate; `count()` and `sum()` add up; `min()` and `max()` combine; an average needs `sum()` and `count()` per window; `quantile(...)`, `uniq(...)`, `count(DISTINCT ...)` and `topK(...)` do not merge across windows, so keep those to one window or add filters. For a template whose time filter is `{{start_time}}`/`{{end_time}}`, pass each window as `start_time` = `from` and `end_time` = `to` instead. When `query` splits such a template itself (its description names the two shapes), `notes` says to call `query` once instead, and the windows are only a fallback. At most 200 windows are returned; `more_windows` counts the older ones the range still holds. More windows than you will run means the range needs rethinking: narrow the time filter, add filters on `raw` before extracting JSON, or set `sampling=` to `suggested_sampling` to estimate rather than measure. A window marked `oversized` holds more than the budget in a single second: add filters or `sampling=` for it
- `unsized` — the query's shape cannot be sized; `explanation` says what to change

With `run` or `windows`:
- `hot_tail` (never for a `{{source}}` template or a query that reads the hot collection itself with `remote()`) — the newest rows of the range are still in the hot collection, which `s3Cluster` holds only once they leave it: `from` is the oldest row still there (Live tail's first row on disk), `estimated_rows` how many of the range's rows that is, `collection` the hot collection to read them from when the row type names one; the top-level `estimated_rows` and the windows then count S3 rows only. Run the same query against `remote(<collection>)` with the time filter unchanged and no `_row_type` filter, and merge it in as one more window. The windows deliberately read past `from`, so a row uploaded to S3 since then is in both legs: add `AND dt < <from>` to them when the merged `count()` or `sum()` has to be exact. Without `from` the boundary could not be probed and the range merely reaches into the last hours
- `hot_rows` (a `{{source}}` template, or a query that reads the hot collection itself, whose range is over the budget with its hot rows counted) — how many rows of the range are still in the hot collection: the query reads them too, but `estimated_rows` and the budget leave them out, since a hot read is usually fast. Without `hot_rows`, `estimated_rows` counts them. If the query still times out on them, the timeout lists windows that split them
- `suggested_sampling` — with more windows than you will run, the `sampling=` rate at which the whole range fits one call

- `... AS time` — the time bucket (e.g., `{{time}} AS time` in a template, or `toStartOfHour(dt) AS time`)
- `... AS value` — the numeric metric (e.g., `count() AS value`)
- `... AS series` — optional: a grouping column for multiple series (e.g., `service AS series`)

**IMPORTANT (line/bar): Always choose a time granularity that produces 50–500 data points** (`{{time}}` picks 30 seconds to 2 hours from the range, which is in that band up to a day but gives more points on longer ranges: bucket by hand there) — too few points make the chart useless, too many make it unreadable. Use these rules based on the query's time range:
- Up to 1 hour → `toStartOfMinute(dt) AS time` → ~60 points
- 1–24 hours → `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 5 MINUTE) AS time` → up to 288 points
- 1–7 days → `toStartOfHour(dt) AS time` → up to 168 points
- 7–30 days → `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 4 HOUR) AS time` → up to 180 points
- 30–90 days → `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 12 HOUR) AS time` → up to 180 points
- 90+ days → `toStartOfDay(dt) AS time`

Additional query instructions (data access patterns) are in:
- `query_help` — logs and spans
- `errors_query_help` — errors
- `metrics_query_help` — metrics

Before a query over more than a few hours of logs, spans or other events, call `query_windows` with the same arguments: it says whether the range fits one call and, if not, the time windows that do.

tools.name: betterstack-ryno__upsert_catalog_records
tools.description:
Add or update a catalog relation's records, keyed by their primary values, so running the same sync
again updates instead of duplicating. A record whose primary values equal a row's is updated: the
added attributes the row names are replaced, the others are left alone. A row no record matches
becomes a new record. One invalid row fails the whole call and writes nothing. Up to 100
records per call. See `catalog_relations` for how the catalog works.

Name `Dependencies` and `Connections` by the other records' primary values.

## Rules

- Name primary attributes after metadata keys incidents really carry. Check recent incidents' metadata with `incidents` and `incident` first: a key no incident carries never matches.
- Reference teams, team members, escalation policies and other Better Stack objects as objects, like `{"type": "Team", "name": "Platform"}`, never as their names in text.
- Never invent records. Every row comes from a source the user pointed you to (code, Terraform, Kubernetes, a Backstage catalog, the service map) or from the user.
- Prefer `upsert_catalog_records` to removing records and adding them again: it keeps every record it doesn't name, while removing them all empties the relation.

records.description: Each record maps attribute names to values: text, an object like {"type": "Team", "name": "Platform"}, or a list of them; an empty list, null or blank text is an empty cell. Like [{"service": "checkout", "Owner": {"type": "Team", "name": "Payments"}, "Dependencies": ["payments-db"], "Type": "Backend"}]

relation_id.description: The ID of the catalog relation (from catalog_relations)

tools.risk_rationale: destructiveHint=true, idempotentHint=true; adds or updates catalog records (keyed by primary value, safe to re-run), a bulk data write that feeds incident metadata enrichment and escalation routing, medium.
